May 2018Cape Flattery, Washington

Cape Flattery, WA

memories below

Edge of the Map

Keep heading northwest in the lower 48 and eventually you run out of country. The last corner of it is Cape Flattery, at the tip of the Olympic Peninsula, and it is a long drive from anywhere. Over Memorial Day weekend I made the trip out with Will, and on the way we stopped in Sekiu, a fishing village on the Strait of Juan de Fuca, to send the drone up over the harbor. The whole bay glittered. The cape itself sits on Makah land, a short drive past the town of Neah Bay. You need a recreation pass to park at the trailhead, so pick one up in town and be a good guest out there. The trail is short, under a mile each way, but it dives into the forest and stays there: big spruce and ferns, roots across the path, long stretches of plank boardwalk, and sunlight slanting through the trunks.

Then the trees part and the land just stops. Below the viewpoints, the Pacific has carved the coast into coves and hollows, with tree-topped stacks standing in dark water and surf swirling around mossy rocks. Tatoosh Island sits just offshore, low and flat. The name Flattery goes back to Captain Cook, who in 1778 noticed an opening in the coastline that flattered him with the hope of a harbor. He sailed on past, but the name stuck. Seen from above, the rock looks even stranger: narrow fins standing in turquoise water, with the surf folding white around them.

We stayed for the sunset. Wind-bent spruce leaned out over the edge, and the sun slid toward Tatoosh through a band of haze while a couple of cameras ran time-lapses. The sky deepened from gold to blue, with contrails scratched across it, and one thin orange line hung on the horizon long after the sun was gone. We stood where a whole continent runs out. Behind us lay every road and city; ahead lay nothing but ocean, all the way to Asia.
